activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
knowledge_domain: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
fact: Day and night are opposites.
story:
Leah held her doll tight. "Daddy, look! Big cart!" Daddy pushed the big cart. Leah walked slow, slow, slow. Then she saw the bakery, and she ran fast, fast, fast.

Daddy picked up bread with a big glove. "Hot," he said. Leah felt the warm air with her hand. Then they went to the freezer. Leah touched the cold glass. "Frozen peas!" she whispered. The peas were cold, cold, cold.

Leah found a little doll. A small doll for her big doll! Daddy said yes. Outside, the sky was dark. "Is it morning?" Leah asked. Daddy shook his head. "It is night. Night is the opposite of day." Leah looked up. The dark sky was full of stars. She hugged both dolls. "Night night, stars," she whispered. The car door went click.

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
fact: In a very dark room, it is hard to tell what color things are.
story:
Miles sat at the art table. He wanted to paint a big apple. Apples are red, he thought. "I need the red paint," he said.

The paint jars lived in the art closet. The closet was very dark. Miles reached in. He felt a jar. He carried it to his table.

Uh oh. The jar was green, not red. Green paint made a green apple. "That is not right," said Miles.

He went back to the dark closet. He felt another jar. It was blue. Blue paint made a blue apple. Outside, a dog barked. The dog pushed its nose on the window. Miles laughed so much he felt dizzy.

Then Miss Kay came. She opened the curtains. Sun lit up the closet. Now Miles could see every jar. He found the red one all by himself. He painted one red apple, one green apple, and one blue one too.

activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
knowledge_domain: searching for a lost favorite toy
fact: Searching one room at a time helps you not miss any places.
story:
Xavier lost Bunny at the grocery store. Bunny was soft and gray. Xavier ran to the fruit area. No Bunny there. He ran to the bread area. No Bunny there. He ran past the milk. He ran past the eggs. "I looked everywhere!" he said.

Mama held his hand. "Let's go slow," she said. "We look at one aisle at a time." Xavier walked down aisle one. He looked up. He looked down. He looked under the apples. No Bunny. Aisle two. He looked behind the big boxes. No Bunny. Aisle three. He looked and looked.

There! Bunny sat by the soup cans. "You were hiding!" said Xavier. He hugged Bunny tight. "Bunny wants lunch," said Mama with a smile. "Bunny speaks soup language," said Xavier. Mama laughed. They put Bunny and three soup cans in the cart.

activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
knowledge_domain: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
fact: Dress-up clothes help you pretend to be someone else.
story:
Kinsley went to Mia's house. Mia had a big toy box. "Let's play house," said Mia.

Mia put a blanket over a chair. It made a little house. Kinsley picked up a teddy bear. "The baby is sleepy," she said. She patted the bear's back. The bear did not wake up.

Then the bear began to cry. Mia made a crying sound. "The baby needs a doctor!" said Kinsley. But Kinsley did not feel like a doctor. She was just Kinsley in her play clothes.

Mia ran to the dress-up box. She pulled out a white coat. "Put this on," she said. Kinsley slid her arms in. Now she looked like a doctor. She stood up tall. "I will help the baby," she said.

Kinsley checked the bear with a toy spoon. "The baby needs a hat," she said. Mia found a tiny sock and put it on the bear's head. The crying stopped. "All better," said Kinsley. Then the two doctors cleaned up the little house. Kinsley left the white coat on.

At the door, Mia waved. "Bye, Doctor Kinsley."

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
knowledge_domain: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
fact: Loud and quiet are opposites.
story:
Julia stood in the kitchen. Her baby brother Sam was asleep. Mama was at the stove. The stove was hot, so Julia stayed back.

Julia wanted to play her drum. She hit it. BANG! BANG! It was loud. The loud sound woke Sam up. He cried and cried.

Mama held Sam. Julia felt bad. She looked at her drum. Then she tapped it. Tap. Tap. It was quiet. Sam stopped crying. His eyes closed. Mama put him down softly.

Julia tapped her drum again. Tap. Tap. The kitchen stayed quiet. The big drum could be loud. The big drum could be quiet too. Julia liked quiet better right now.

Then Julia saw something small and gray by the window. A little bird sat there. It sang one soft note. Julia tapped her drum slow, so slow. The bird sang back fast, so fast. Julia giggled. She played quiet and slow, all the way to the end.

Mama smiled. "Snack time," she said. Julia got a cold cup of milk. The milk was cold, and her warm cookie smelled good. She sat next to Sam. Everyone was happy.

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
fact: Sorting by color means putting all the things that are the same color together in one group.
story:
Nova loved art class. Today she painted a cow. She made the cow brown with big black spots. Her paper was high up on the easel. She dipped her brush in red, blue and yellow paint. Red made her think of apples. Blue made her think of the sky.

Then the teacher said, "Clean-up time!" Nova put the caps on the paint. Sam made piles of blocks on the rug. He made a red pile, a blue pile and a yellow pile. Nova looked at the red pile. One block there was yellow. It was hiding in the wrong spot! Nova picked it out. She set it down with the other yellow blocks.

Sam looked at his piles. He smiled big. "Yellow goes with yellow," he said. Nova smiled too. She could hear the paint brushes drip drip in the water cups. Someday she dreamed she would paint a purple cow. For now she picked up the last blue block and put it with its friends.

activity: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
knowledge_domain: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
fact: The lowercase letters b and d look alike but face opposite ways.
story:
Charles sat at the book club with his friend Mila. Miss Jo held up a big card. It had the word dog on it. Charles looked and looked. Then he laughed. "That says bog!" he said.

Mila laughed too. "Silly! A bog is not an animal." Charles looked again. He made a b with his finger. Then he made a d. The round parts did not face the same way. "Oh!" he said. He turned his b around. Now it was a d. "D, d, dog!" he said.

Miss Jo clapped. "Try one more, Charles." The card said bed. Charles checked the round parts. He counted, "One round this way, one round that way." He said, "B, e, d. Bed!" His itchy sock needed a scratch, but he kept reading. "Dog, bed, dog, bed," said Charles, and everyone cheered.

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
knowledge_domain: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
fact: Your tongue can taste that a lemon is sour.
story:
Raphael took his old truck to the doctor's office. He could not wait to show it to Doctor Maya. "Today we check your eyes," she said. Raphael looked with his eyes. He saw a red chart on the wall. "I see an A!" he shouted.

Then Doctor Maya held up a small yellow lemon slice. "Open wide," she said. Raphael thought lemons taste like orange juice, sweet and good. He opened his mouth. His tongue touched the lemon. WOW! His whole face scrunched up. "Sour!" he cried. "So sour!" Doctor Maya laughed. "Your tongue can taste that," she said.

Next, Raphael heard a beep with his ears. He sniffed a sticker with his nose. It smelled like strawberries. He touched his truck with his fingers. It felt bumpy. At last he stuck out his tongue for one more tiny taste. "Sour again!" he said, and he giggled and giggled.

activity: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
knowledge_domain: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
fact: Some songs have hand actions, like the spider climbing up in 'The Itsy Bitsy Spider.'
story:
Kai stood in the garage with Dad. Dad turned on a song. It had a big, steady beat. Boom, boom, boom.

Kai wanted to clap along. He clapped too fast. "Slow down, silly!" Dad laughed. Kai chased the beat with his hands. He clapped again. This time his claps landed just right. Clap, clap, clap. The song went boom and his hands went clap. They matched!

"Now let's sing the spider song," said Dad. Kai loved that song. It had hand actions. He made his fingers climb up, up, up the spout. Then he made the spider climb down. Dad froze like a statue. "Wait! Where is your spider going?" Kai giggled. He had mixed it up! The rain comes down, but the spider climbs up. He tried again. His fingers went up, up, up. Then down came the rain, and his fingers swooshed low.

Mom came into the garage. She clapped along with them. Kai sang the whole song all by himself. His fingers climbed and the beat went boom. Mom gave him a big hug. "One more time!" said Kai. His spider climbed up, up, up again.

activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
knowledge_domain: spending a surprise snow day at home
fact: Wet mittens and boots are left out to dry after playing in the snow.
story:
Amelia woke up and saw white. Snow had come in the night. "A snow day!" said Mom. "No school today."

Amelia put on her boots and her red mittens. She went out to the backyard. She patted the snow. She made a small snowman with a stick for an arm. From the fence she could see the train go by, all covered in white. "Pretty," said Amelia.

Then Mom called her in for warm milk. Amelia pulled off her boots. Water dripped on the floor. Her mittens were soaked too.

"I want to go back out," said Amelia. She picked up her mittens. They were cold and wet. "Yuck," said Amelia.

"Let's put them here," said Mom. They hung the mittens on the chair by the warm vent. The boots went under it. Mom held the warm milk, and Amelia drank it all up.

Later Amelia touched her mittens. They were dry! She slid them on. She put on her boots. They were dry too.

"Back to the snowman," said Amelia. Mom smiled and opened the door.

activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
knowledge_domain: searching for a lost favorite toy
fact: A flashlight helps you see into dark spots, like under a bed.
story:
Mateo was going to the car. "My blue dinosaur!" he shouted. "He is lost!" Mateo loved that dinosaur. He could not leave it alone at home.

He looked on the car floor. He looked by his feet. "I see dust," said Mateo. "I see one old cookie. No dinosaur." He looked under the seat. It was too dark. He could not see anything at all.

"I can't see!" said Mateo. "The dark spot is too dark!" Mom smiled. She reached into her bag. She took out a flashlight. Mom clicked it on. The light was bright. "Here you go," she said.

Mateo pointed the flashlight under the seat. The dark spot was not dark anymore. He saw his dinosaur! "I see his tail! I see his hair!" Mateo laughed. He reached in and pulled. Out came the dinosaur, all dusty and happy.

Mateo hugged him tight. "You were under the seat! The light found you!" He held the flashlight up high. "Mom, can we look for more things?" Mom laughed too. "Maybe we can sell cookies at the big sale," she said. "But first, let's buckle the dinosaur in." Mateo clicked the seat belt over the dinosaur. "There," said Mateo. "Now you ride with me."

activity: getting a first haircut at a salon
knowledge_domain: getting a first haircut at a salon
fact: Sitting very still helps the hairdresser cut your hair neatly.
story:
Luke went to the mall with his dad. Luke was getting his very first haircut. The salon had a big fish tank. The fish were orange and blue.

A lady named May put a low stool by her chair. "Hop up," she said. Luke sat down. May sprayed warm water on his hair. It felt like soft rain.

Luke saw a fish swim by. He turned his head to look. Snip went the scissors. May had to fix the same spot twice. "Hmm," said Luke. "What happens if I sit very still?" He tried it. He sat like a statue. He watched only the mirror. Snip, snip, snip. The hair fell down like soft snow. It tickled his nose.

"Can I bring the fish a magnet?" Luke asked his dad. Dad laughed. "Fish don't want magnets," he said. "They want fish food." May turned the chair around. Luke looked in the mirror. His hair was neat and short. All even, all around. "I look like a big boy," said Luke. He held the mirror himself and smiled.

activity: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
knowledge_domain: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
fact: Pressing too hard on a pencil can break its tip.
story:
Ava sat at the big table in writing club. Her paper was yellow like a bee. Miss Jo gave her a pencil. "Now we write your name," said Miss Jo. Ava wanted to write AVA all by herself.

Ava held the pencil tight. She pressed down very hard. She made a big A. Then she made a V. Then the pencil tip went SNAP. The little black point fell onto the paper. "Oh no!" said Ava. "My pencil broke!"

Tommy laughed, but not in a mean way. "That happened to me too," he said. Miss Jo gave Ava a new pencil. "Try again," she said. Ava held it soft this time. She pressed gently, gently. She made a A. She made a V. She made another A. No snap! The letters stayed on the paper.

"Look, look!" said Ava. "A V A! That is me!" She jumped up so fast her chair went wobble. "Careful," said Miss Jo with a smile, "or you will lock that chair under the table." Ava giggled. She sat back down and wrote her name one more time, soft as a bee landing on a flower. "I can write all day," said Ava, "if I press like this."

activity: going to the dentist for the first time
knowledge_domain: going to the dentist for the first time
fact: A dentist wears gloves when putting fingers or tools in your mouth.
story:
Harper held Mama's hand at the big blue door. "This is the dentist," said Mama. Inside there was a soft chair, and a small gray toy mouse sat on the counter.

A kind dentist came in. "Hello, Harper," she said. "One, two, three fingers up. Now I will count your teeth." Harper saw the dentist's hands were blue. "Your hands are blue!" said Harper.

The dentist pulled at her fingers. Snap went one glove. Snap went the other. Underneath, her hands were not blue at all. She slid the gloves back on, one by one, and they were smooth and clean.

"Now open wide," said the dentist. Harper opened her mouth like a little mouse opening for cheese. The dentist counted, "One tooth, two teeth, ten teeth!" Her gloved fingers tapped each one, so soft and gentle.

Harper squeezed the gray mouse toy. "All done," said the dentist. "You were so brave."

"Can I wear blue gloves too?" asked Harper.

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
knowledge_domain: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
fact: Your feet can feel things too, like soft grass under bare toes.
story:
Matteo wanted to find the best spot at the park. He looked with his eyes. He saw a big tree and a red slide. He heard a dog bark with his ears. He smelled flowers with his nose. "The flowers smell sweet," he said.

Then Matteo saw a berry bush. "Can I taste one?" he asked. Mama said, "No, those are not for eating. Here, take this apple instead." Matteo took a bite. "Sweet!" he said. He touched the apple with his hands. It was smooth and cool.

Near the tree, Matteo saw soft green grass. He sat down and took off his shoes. He wiggled his toes. The grass tickled his feet! "My feet can feel it too," he said. He laughed and stomped. "Tickle, tickle, tickle!" Mama came to sit by him. "This is the best spot," said Matteo. He put his careful hands in the grass and wiggled his toes again.

activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
knowledge_domain: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
fact: A big circle and a tiny circle are both circles, because size does not change a shape.
story:
Levi ran to the shape table at school. A big red clock sat there. It was round like a ball.

"My button is small," said Mia. "It can't be a circle like the big clock."

Levi held up his tiny button. He spun it on the table. It rolled and rolled. The big clock was round too. He put the button next to the clock. Both were round! Levi clapped his hands.

"They are both circles!" said Mia.

Levi looked for more circles. He found a little round cracker. He found a big round hoop outside. The cracker fit in his hand. Levi had to stand inside the hoop. Big circle, tiny circle. They were still circles!

Then Levi found square blocks and a triangle roof. He stacked them fast. A rectangle door went at the bottom.

"Look at my new animal house!" he said.

A toy cat walked in. "The cat can stay here," said Levi. He drew a tiny round door for a mouse, too.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
fact: A stove can be hot even when it does not look hot, so only grown-ups touch it.
story:
Elizabeth went to the park with Grandma. She saw a big black grill near the picnic table. Smoke came up from it. "Who made the smoke?" she wondered.

A man came to cook on the grill. Elizabeth wanted to see close. Grandma held her hand. "Stay with me," Grandma said. Elizabeth stood by Grandma and looked from far away.

The man put a hot dog on the grill. It went sizzle, sizzle. Elizabeth clapped her hands. The hot dog began to turn brown. She saw that the fire made the hot dog hot. Then the man turned a knob. The fire went away. "Is it cold now?" Elizabeth wondered. She did not touch. She asked the man instead. The man shook his head. "Only I touch it," he said. He waved his hand over the top. He kept his hand high, not on it.

The hot dog was ready. The man put it in a bun. He gave it time to cool. Then he handed it to Grandma. Grandma broke a little piece for Elizabeth. It was warm and soft now. Elizabeth took a gentle little bite.

Some ducks walked by in a line. "They look like a class going to school," said Elizabeth. Grandma laughed. Elizabeth waved at the ducks. "Hello, class!" she said.

activity: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
knowledge_domain: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
fact: Learning to zip your own coat takes practice.
story:
Thomas put on his red coat. He pulled the zipper up. It stuck near his tummy. He tried again. It stuck again.

"Let's practice at the store," said Mom. "It is cold by the freezers."

They walk to the grocery store. First they pick apples. Then they walk down the milk line of the store. The freezer aisle was very cold. Thomas pulled his zipper again. It went up a tiny bit. Then it stopped. "Keep trying," said Mom. Thomas pulled it again. Up it went, a little more. Then it stopped at his chin. He tugged hard. The zipper closed all the way. His coat was warm and neat.

"Look, Mom! I did it!" said Thomas. Mom clapped. They walked to the cold freezer. Thomas got to pick the ice cream. He held the cold box in his warm hands.

On the way home, Thomas zipped his coat all by himself again. "Zip," he said. "Zip, zip."

activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
knowledge_domain: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
fact: When someone is talking, we listen and wait until they finish.
story:
Avery went to the store with Dad. She wanted the big red apples by the window. She saw them right away.

Dad was talking to the fruit man. "Avery waited. But she wanted to talk so much. She pulled Dad's sleeve. Dad held up one finger. So Avery waited some more. The fruit man stopped talking. Then Dad said, "Yes, Avery?" She said, "Can we get apples?" Dad smiled. "Yes, we can."

At the meat counter, a man had a sharp knife. The man cut the ham. Dad kept Avery back a safe step. She watched the knife go up and down. The man gave Dad the ham. Then it was their turn. Avery said, "Thank you," all by herself.

In the checkout line, a phone rang. The lady at the register answered it. "Why is she talking on the phone?" Avery asked. Dad said, "Someone called her. We wait." So they waited. The lady finished, and she said, "Your turn now." Avery put the apples on the belt. They went round and round. Outside, the wind made the bags dance. Avery held Dad's hand all the way home.

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
knowledge_domain: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
fact: You can often smell dinner cooking before you see it.
story:
Jacob sat in the big chair at the doctor's office. The doctor smiled at him. "Let's check your eyes," she said. Jacob used his eyes to see a picture of a river on the wall. The water looked blue and cold.

"Now your ears." Jacob used his ears to hear the doctor's bell. Ding! Then she looked in his nose. "Sniff like a puppy," she said. Jacob sniffed. Then he opened his mouth, and she peeked at his tongue.

At home, Jacob played with his blocks. He sniffed the air. "Soup!" he said. "I smell soup!" He ran to the kitchen. There it was, bubbling on the stove, where Dad stood. "You smelled it before you saw it," said Dad. Jacob laughed. "My nose remembers soup." Dad gave him a soft piece of bread. Jacob touched it with his fingers. It was warm. "I will get you a blanket," Dad said, "because you look tired and a little weak." Jacob ate his bread and smiled. "Good nose," he said to himself, and he patted his own nose.

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
knowledge_domain: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
fact: The printed words in a book say the same thing every time the book is read.
story:
Aubrey wanted the bunny book at daycare. But Ben had it first. Ben sat on the rug and held the book upside down.

"Can I read it too?" Aubrey asked.

"Okay," said Ben. "But I can't read the words yet."

Miss Jo came over. "I can read it," she said. She turned the book around. She opened the front cover first. Then she began.

"One little bunny hopped down the road," Miss Jo read.

Aubrey peeked at the page. She saw the little black words. Then Ben's big sister came in to help. She read the same book to them later.

"One little bunny hopped down the road," she read.

Aubrey sat up fast. "You said the same words!" she said. "The same as Miss Jo!"

The big sister smiled. "The words stay on the page," she said.

Aubrey turned to the next page. She pointed at the words. "Now say this part," she said.

So the big sister read it. Aubrey listened and looked. Then she held the book herself. She turned one page, then the next, all the way to the back.

"Again!" said Ben.

"The end," Aubrey read, pointing at the last page.

activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
knowledge_domain: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
fact: Friends playing pretend together can agree on what happens next.
story:
Ella was at daycare. She wanted to play pretend with Leo. Leo had a big toy dragon.

Ella hugged the dragon. "The dragon is nice," she said.

Leo shook his head. "The dragon is scary," he said.

Ella made a sad face. "Can we both be right?" she asked.

Leo thought. "Maybe," he said. "The dragon is scary to bad guys. But he is nice to us."

Ella smiled. "Yes! A friendly dragon." The dragon gave Leo a pretend scratch on his arm. Leo laughed.

Then the dragon got an owie. Ella put a bandage on it. Leo used pretend glue to stick a paper wing back on. Ella patted the dragon. "There, there," she said. "All better."

The friendly dragon flew them both home to the playhouse for a snack.

activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
knowledge_domain: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
fact: Rain boots keep your feet dry when you step in puddles.
story:
Nora looked out the window. "It is rainy today!" she said. Big drops went plip, plip, plip.

Nora wanted to jump in puddles. She grabbed her orange rain boots. But one boot was missing! She looked under her bed. She looked behind the turtle tank. No boot.

Nora wore her sneakers instead. She ran outside. The wind blew her hat off. She splashed in a big puddle. Splash! Her socks got soggy. Water squished in her shoes. "Oh no," said Nora. "My feet are all wet."

She ran back inside. There was the boot, under the table! Nora pulled it on. She put on the other boot too. She ran out again. Splash! This time her feet stayed dry. "Dry feet, dry feet!" she shouted. Then she painted a picture of the rainy day.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: Each team wears its own colors so you can tell the two teams apart.
story:
Isaiah sat on the big couch. His dad sat next to him. Auntie May was there too. The TV showed a game with running people.

Isaiah pointed at the TV. "Who has the ball now?" he asked. He could not tell. All the people looked mixed up to him. He squeezed his dad's arm.

"Look at the shirts," Dad said. "One team wears red. One team wears blue." Isaiah looked hard. A red shirt spun around with the ball. A blue shirt ran after him. Now Isaiah could see them apart. "Red has it!" he shouted. His smile grew wide.

Auntie May clapped. "Good eyes, Isaiah!" she said. Isaiah watched the red shirts and blue shirts run up and down. He lost a tooth last week, and he showed everyone his new gap when he laughed.

Then a blue shirt took the ball and kicked it far. The net moved. Everyone jumped up. Isaiah jumped too, right on the soft rug. Dad caught his hand so he would not fall.

"Red can still score," said Dad. Isaiah sat close to him. He knew just who to watch now. "Go red team!" he called.

activity: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
knowledge_domain: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
fact: Covering your ears with your hands makes sounds seem quieter.
story:
Max sat at Grandma's big table. He wanted to play the senses game. Grandma said, "Ears hear. What do ears hear?"

Just then a big truck went by. It rumbled loud. Max put his hands over his ears. The rumble got quieter. He took his hands off. The rumble got loud again. He put his hands back on. Quiet again.

"Grandma!" said Max. "My hands make it quiet!"

Grandma smiled. "Yes, your ears were covered. Can your nose cover too?"

Max shook his head. "Noses smell," he said. "My nose smells your cookies!" His tummy felt happy.

Grandma put a warm cookie on his plate. Max looked at it with his eyes. "Eyes see the cookie," he said. Then he touched the plate. It was smooth. "Hands feel it!"

He took a little bite. "Tongue tastes it! That's all five!"

Grandma clapped. "You didn't miss one."

Max felt brave and proud. "Tomorrow can we play again?" he asked.

"Yes," said Grandma. "And maybe next time, the ocean sounds on my radio."

Max giggled and covered his ears, then peeked out with a smile.

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
knowledge_domain: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
fact: A tag on a pet's collar tells people how to reach its family if the pet gets lost.
story:
Ivy walked home with Dad. She held the little box with two hands. Inside was her new puppy, Pip.

Pip had a soft collar. Ivy did not like it. "It is ugly," she said. The collar was old and gray. Dad smiled. "We can get a new one at the shop." At the shop, Ivy picked a red collar. Then Dad showed her a small tag. Ivy held the tag in her hand. It had words on it. It had their phone number too.

"Why the number?" Ivy asked. Dad said, "Put it on and see." So they did. The tag went click on the red collar.

The next day, Pip wriggled out the door. He ran down the street! Ivy called and called. Then a kind woman walked up with Pip in her arms. "I saw the tag," she said. "I called the number. It is your puppy!" Ivy hugged Pip tight. She patted the little tag. It went click, click on the red collar.

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
knowledge_domain: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
fact: The word 'five' and the numeral 5 mean the same number.
story:
Arya went to the library with her dad. She wanted a book about ducks. The duck books were not on their shelf. "Hmm," said Arya. "Where did they go?"

She saw a sign with a big 5 on it. Arya held up her hand. She counted her fingers. "One, two, three, four, five," she said. The sign said five too. "The five on the sign is my five!" she said. Her dad laughed. "You found it," he said.

Arya counted her steps to the room with the 5. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven," she said. She walked in. There were the duck books on the top shelf. A boy was singing a counting song. "Five little ducks went out one day," he sang. Arya sang along. She picked a duck book and let dad carry it. "Ten little duck toes," said Arya. "Salty duck feet?" said Dad. "No, silly," said Arya. "Ducks are not salty."

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: A coach teaches the team and helps the players learn the game.
story:
Rosalie stood by the big blue pool. Her swim team was called the Little Fish. She put on her flat pink flippers. The water smelled like sunshine and chlorine.

Coach Dana blew her whistle. "Fish, line up on the wall!" All the kids found a spot. But Rosalie did not know where to stand. She stood in the middle, all alone.

"Rosalie, come stand next to me," said Coach Dana. She pointed to the wall. Rosalie walked over and put her hand on the warm tiles. "Now kick like this," said Coach Dana. She splashed her legs in the light water. Rosalie kicked too. Splish, splash! Her feet made white bubbles.

"Look at that!" said Rosalie. "You kick, and you go forward!" Coach Dana clapped her hands. "Kick, kick, kick!" said Coach Dana. Rosalie kicked all the way to the rope.

"Did you see me swim?" Rosalie called to her mom. Mom waved from her chair. Rosalie turned around and kicked back to the wall. The water went swish, swish, swish behind her.

activity: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
knowledge_domain: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
fact: A new baby must be touched very gently.
story:
Ali sat on the big back step. Mom sat next to him with a bundle. Inside was his new baby sister. Her name was Nia. Ali wanted to pat her head. He patted her, but too hard. Nia's face scrunched up. She began to cry. Ali felt like he might lose his happy day.

Mom took Ali's hand. "Try like this," she said. She moved his hand slow and soft. Ali stroked Nia's tiny fingers. He used one finger, very gently. Nia stopped crying. Her eyes found Ali's face.

Mom smiled. "She likes that," Mom said. Ali stroked again, soft as a feather. Nia's little hand wrapped around his finger. Ali grinned. "She is holding me," he said. Mom kissed the top of his head.

activity: getting a first haircut at a salon
knowledge_domain: getting a first haircut at a salon
fact: Cutting hair does not hurt.
story:
Anthony sat in the car. "We will meet Miss Kim today," said Mom. "She cuts hair." Anthony held his hat down tight. "Scissors are sharp," he said. "Will they hurt my head?" "Let's go and see," said Mom.

At the salon, Anthony sat in a big chair. It went up and up. Miss Kim picked up her scissors. Snip, snip. Anthony squeezed his eyes shut. Then he waited. But he did not feel anything at all. He opened one eye. A little piece of hair fell down. It floated like a tiny feather. Snip, snip, more hair fell. Still no hurt! Anthony laughed.

"Look," said Miss Kim. She held up a mirror. Anthony saw a short, pretty haircut. "It tickles," he said. "Can we keep the hair?" Mom put some in her pocket. Then Anthony waved and ran to the car.

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
knowledge_domain: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
fact: Chocolate can make dogs very sick, so dogs are never given chocolate.
story:
Riley held the little dog's leash. The vet smiled and said, "His name is Biscuit." Riley wanted to give Biscuit a treat right away. She dug in her pocket. She found her chocolate coin. "Here, Biscuit," she said.

The vet shook her head. "Not that one. Chocolate can make dogs very sick." She handed Riley a small dog treat instead. "Try this." Riley held it out flat on her hand. Biscuit sniffed it. He sniffed it again. Riley waited. She waited some more, watching the cloudy sky out the window.

At last Biscuit took the treat. His tail wagged and wagged. "Good boy," said Riley. In the corner, a green snake sat in a glass tank. Riley waved at it too. Then she and Biscuit walked home together, one slow step at a time.

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
knowledge_domain: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
fact: Open and closed are opposites, like a door that is open or shut.
story:
Elena went to the park with Dad. She had a new juice box in the cooler. She wanted it cold. Dad opened the cooler. Then a big dog ran by, fast. Elena watched the dog. The cooler stayed open. The sun was hot. It shone right in.

Later Elena drank her juice. It was warm now. Warm, not cold. She made a sad face. "It got warm in the sun," she said. Dad nodded. "The lid was open."

They got one more juice box from home. Elena held it. It felt so cold in her hands. Dad put it in the cooler. Elena pushed the lid. Click. It was closed. She pulled it open. She pushed it shut again. Open, shut, open, shut.

"You can draw the lid on paper," said Dad. "What will you name your picture?" Elena smiled. "Cold juice." She sat down by the little tree. She waited. Slow waiting, then a sip. The juice was still cold. "Yum," said Elena, and she gave the lid one more click.

activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
knowledge_domain: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
fact: When you play house, each person can pick a role, like the parent or the baby.
story:
Jasmine ran to the playground with her toy rabbit. Her friend Mia was already there. Mia had a small teddy bear and a big toy pot.

"Let's play house," said Mia. Jasmine smiled big. "I will be the mama," said Jasmine. "No, I want to be the mama," said Mia. Both girls held their toys tight. Nobody moved. The house had no mama at all.

Then Jasmine had an idea. "You be the mama now," she said. "I can be the baby later." Mia nodded. "Okay! We can switch." Mia stirred leaves in the pot. She mixed them with a stick. "Time to eat, little rabbit," she said in a mama voice. Jasmine made her rabbit hop to the pot. "Yum, yum," said the rabbit.

Mia patted the teddy bear's head. "Sleep now, baby bear," she sang. The friendly sun went behind a cloud, like a blanket for the sky. "Switch time!" said Jasmine. Jasmine became the mama. She rocked the rabbit and sang a soft song. "My turn to mix the soup," she said. She stirred and stirred. "More, please," said Mia in a tiny baby voice. Jasmine gave her a leaf cookie. "All gone," said the baby.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
fact: Never put fingers or things into an electrical outlet.
story:
Declan wanted to wash his hands all by himself. He stood at the sink and looked up. The faucet was high, high up. "Can I do it, Mama?" he asked. "I will stay right here with you," said Mama.

Mama turned the faucet. First came cold water. Declan touched the stream. Brrr, it was cold like ice! Then Mama turned it a tiny bit the other way. The water got warm. Declan felt the warm water on his hands. One turn made cold. Another turn made warm. How did that happen? He turned his head to see the pipes.

Then he saw something on the wall. It was a small white face with two little holes. It looked shy, hiding near the sink. What was it? Declan pointed at it. "Mama, what is that?"

"That is an outlet," said Mama. "Fingers never go in there. Only plugs go in." Declan looked at his wet fingers. He kept them far, far away. He put them in the warm water instead.

"I build with my fingers," said Declan. "And I paint with my fingers too."

"Yes," said Mama. "So we keep them safe." She gave him a soft towel. Declan dried each finger, one by one. Then he waved at the little white face on the wall.

"Bye bye, outlet," he said.

activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
knowledge_domain: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
fact: Folding a square piece of paper in half, edge to edge, makes a rectangle.
story: Emile sat at the little table at daycare. He was making a house from paper shapes. He had a red circle for the sun. He had a blue square for the house. He had a green triangle for the roof. But he needed a door. A door is a rectangle. He looked in the shape box. There was no rectangle left. "I wish I had a door," said Emile. Then he saw a white square napkin. He picked it up. He folded it in half, edge to edge. He pressed it flat with his hand. He opened his fingers. The square was gone. Now he held a rectangle! "Look at my door," said Emile. He glued it on the house. Mia clapped. "A door," she said. Emile got another napkin. He folded it in half, edge to edge. Another rectangle! He made a mailbox too. Then he put on his shoe and went outside to play.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
fact: Stay where your grown-up can see you when you are out.
story:
Billie went to the playground with Dad. The sun was warm on the slide. The metal slide felt hot under her hand, so she slid down fast and kept her hands up.

Near the fence, Billie saw a shiny can in the grass. She reached out. Dad came quickly and picked it up. "Not for little hands," he said. He put it in the bin. Billie waved bye-bye to the can.

Then Billie saw the big red ball. It rolled far, far away. It went past the trees to the far end of the playground. Billie ran after it. She ran and ran. Then she stopped. She looked back. She could not see Dad. The trees were big. Dad was not there.

Billie stood very still. Then she walked back the way she came. She walked past the trees. She walked past the swings. And there was Dad, waving by the slide. Billie ran to him and held his hand. Dad gave her the red ball. It had rolled all the way back, lazy and slow, in the wind.

"Again!" said Billie.

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
knowledge_domain: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
fact: The counting words always go in the same order: one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten.
story:
Matteo sat in his car seat. He wanted to count the red cars going by. "One, two, four," he said.

His big sister Rosa turned around. "Try again," she said. "Say it with me."

They said it together, slow and loud. "One, two, three, four, five."

A red car zoomed past. "Six, seven!" shouted Matteo.

"Good counting," said Rosa. "Keep going. The words stay in the same line."

Matteo watched the road. A truck. A bus. Three red cars! "Eight, nine, ten!" he yelled.

Mama laughed from the front seat. "Ten red cars! What a big day."

"Now count the blue ones," said Rosa.

Matteo looked out the window. He took a big breath. "One, two, three!"

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: In soccer and basketball, the referee blows a whistle to stop play.
story:
Eloise sat with her dad in the big stadium. Her cousin Mia sat on the other side. The green field below was clean and bright. The players ran and ran after one ball. Eloise pointed. "That team is blue. That team is red. My favorite shirt is red too," she said.

Then a loud sound came. Tweet! Tweet! All the players stopped running. They stood still. Eloise tugged her dad's sleeve. "Why did they stop?" she asked. Mia cupped her hands by her ears. "The whistle did it," she said. Eloise watched the man in black. He put the small whistle to his mouth again. Tweet! The players stopped once more.

Eloise counted on her fingers. "One whistle, they stop. One nod, they go," she said. The game began again. The crowd clapped and roared. Eloise clapped too. "Maybe I will blow a whistle one day," she said. Mia laughed and held her hand.

activity: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
knowledge_domain: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
fact: A coat helps keep your body warm when it is cold outside.
story:
Wyatt was at the grocery store with Mom. The big doors opened. Cold air rushed in. Wyatt bounced on his toes. Brrr!

"Time for your coat," said Mom. Wyatt wanted to do it himself. He pushed one arm in. Wrong hole! He tried again. Yes! Arm one, arm two. Now the zipper. He pulled it up, up, up. It stuck. He tugged hard. Zip! It went all the way to his chin.

"I did it!" said Wyatt. The cold air touched his cheeks. But his body stayed warm inside the coat. He felt like a cozy feather.

Outside, snowflakes started to fall. Wyatt ran to the window. "Look, Mom! Snow!" His zipper was still up. His coat was still warm. "Zip me again tomorrow!" he said.

activity: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
knowledge_domain: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
fact: You can show how old you are by holding up that many fingers.
story:
Miles was four years old today. His family was at the park for his birthday. There was a big table with cake and juice. Balloons bobbed on the chairs.

A boy named Sam came over. Sam had curly hair and a red shirt. "How old are you?" Sam asked.

Miles looked at his hand. He held up three fingers. Sam counted them. "Three?" Sam said. Miles shook his head. That was not right. He thought hard.

Miles put one more finger up. Now he had four fingers in the air. "Four!" said Sam. "I am four too." Sam held up four fingers too. They both laughed. Two hands, four fingers each, side by side.

"Look, Mom," said Miles. "Four!" His mom smiled and gave him a glass of cold juice. It was sweet and cold on his tongue. Sam sat next to him on the bench. Dad lit the birthday candles, way over at the grill table, and everyone sang.

Miles blew out the candles with one big breath. Smoke curled up like a little ribbon. Sam clapped. "Happy birthday, Miles," he said. Miles grinned and held up four fingers one more time.
